papers.title: Beyond Binary Controllability: Reachability Margins for Power Systems via Scalable Screening
papers.summary: This paper studies unreachability screening for power systems, focusing on the inadequate control authority that arises under stressed grid conditions. Its main result is an infeasibility \textit{margin} for linearized differential algebraic equation models that quantifies how far a prescribed terminal target lies from the reachable set in finite time. The paper specifically develops a conic benchmark method together with two first order methods based on projected subgradients and bundle updates for scalably repeated screening. Studies on IEEE benchmark networks show reduced terminal reachability under stressed conditions and tighter actuation limits, while first order methods remain accurate and substantially faster on large systems. Comparisons with standard reachability methods such as CORA further demonstrate the usefulness and scalability of the proposed infeasibility margins. All results and codes are included in a Github repository.

papers.title: Sub Terahertz LEO Satellite Communication: Is Doppler Shift a Major Challenge?
papers.summary: In this work, we investigate the impact of Doppler frequency shift on sub-terahertz low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite communications using OFDM transmission. To comprehensively evaluate the severity of the Doppler shift impact on sub-terahertz satellite-to-ground links, we first put together an evaluation framework that jointly accounts for major Doppler-induced and non-Doppler-induced signal impairments in such systems. We then compare and contrast three possible engineering approaches to deal with Doppler shift in such a communication system. Our study concludes that (i)~while just ignoring the Doppler effect in such high-frequency and high-mobility systems substantially compromises the performance and reliability, (ii)~most of the negative effects can be eliminated by implementing only a small set of low-complexity measures. We particularly show that even a single Doppler shift estimation over a 5-min-long satellite pass over the ground user location may be sufficient to ensure high performance throughout the entire connectivity period. Hence, while Doppler shift is an important effect to account for in sub-terahertz LEO satellite communications, it should not constitute a critical design challenge for these emerging systems.

papers.title: Ranking the Parameters Shaping Grid Dynamics
papers.summary: Generator and transmission line parameters do not shape the time-domain behavior of a power system equally; a parameter that dominates one dynamic property can be almost invisible to another. This paper studies how the physical parameters of a detailed and general nonlinear differential algebraic equation (DAE) grid model shape the properties that decide whether system states such as frequencies, voltages, and angles can be inferred, observed, controlled, and kept stable. The rankings are conditional as they depend on where grid sensors and actuators sit, on the operating region and the disturbance, on the network topology, and on other settings that the operator chooses. The framework combines DAE trajectory sensitivities, variational Gramians, and stability margin sensitivities to measure how much each parameter reshapes the network dynamics. On three benchmark systems, the rankings show where dynamic leverage concentrates and where the control-theoretic metrics disagree, and they point to how parameter studies can guide calibration, sensor and actuator placement, and security assessment. The proposed methods herein are also scalable and can be tested on grids with tens of thousands of buses.

papers.title: The Iberian Blackout: A Black Swan or a Gray Rhino? A Protection-Aware Dynamic Voltage Security Assessment
papers.summary: On 28 April 2025, the Iberian power system collapsed after a rapid voltage rise that led to widespread generation disconnections and loss of synchronism. The final report of the ENTSO-E Expert Panel attributes the blackout to several interacting factors including ineffective voltage control, fixed power factor operation, misaligned protection settings, manual shunt reactor switching, and limited observability. These factors raise a general question: given the current state, can the next trip, ramp, topology action, or shunt switching raise the voltages measured by overvoltage relays above their settings before voltage controls respond? We answer it with a protection-aware dynamic voltage security assessment. For each candidate event, the method computes the voltage at every overvoltage relay over the relay time window from a dynamic model of the network, its controls, and its relays. It predicts which relays trip after a first trip, identifies assets whose relay or measurement data are insufficient for a safety conclusion, and, when one exists, computes a minimum-cost fast reactive power action that keeps all relay voltages below their settings. Case studies on four benchmark systems and a 2000-bus system that reproduces the mechanism of the Iberian blackout show that the method flagged every event that caused a secondary trip within the relay window, never declared safe a plant that tripped within that window, and, on the benchmarks, found fast reactive power actions that prevented the trips within the relay window whenever it judged such actions feasible. These results were validated with nonlinear time-domain simulations. The code is publicly available.

papers.title: Safety Verification for Voltage Control in Inverter Dominated Radial Distribution Networks under Actuator and Sensor Adversarial Attacks
papers.summary: This paper develops a safety verification framework for inverter-based radial distribution networks under sensor and actuator attacks. Each customer is equipped with a droop-based controller to regulate its voltage within a desirable bound of a reference, i.e., to achieve safety. In our setting, attacks and disturbances enter the droop-based controllers, while actuator attacks corrupt the reactive power injected into the network. Consequently, invariance of the controller state alone does not guarantee compliance with inverter capacities or customer voltage limits. To address this challenge, we derive conditions to guarantee that the reactive power state remains inside a predefined ellipsoid, while at the same time ensuring that the attacked reactive power injections and customer voltages respect predetermined operating limits that hold uniformly for the entire predefined ellipsoid. Together, these conditions guarantee safety under all admissible disturbances and state-dependent sensor and actuator attacks. Finally, we express the resulting containment condition as a linear matrix inequality (LMI) feasibility problem. A five-customer radial network based on the CIGRE benchmark corroborates our theoretical developments in simulations.

papers.title: Scaly: an Optimizing Compiler for Optimal Control
papers.summary: We present Scaly, an open-source optimizing compiler for optimal control, written in Python, that generates fast C code. Scaly provides a modeling language embedded in Python for the parametric optimization problems that arise in model predictive control and moving horizon estimation, and computes the sparse derivatives that standard optimization solvers need. Scaly accepts general nonlinear programs but applies optimizations specific to optimal control, which preserve the repeated structure of a problem, such as the stages of a horizon, through differentiation down to the generated loops. The generated C depends only on the C math library and never allocates memory dynamically. On three benchmark problems, Scaly evaluates the Hessian of the Lagrangian up to 26 times faster than CasADi, with smaller binaries and build times that stay nearly constant with the horizon. With the same solver, Scaly shortens the solver time per control step on every benchmark, by a factor of up to 9.

papers.title: Probability-Layer Clustering for Bound-and-Budget Calibration in Multi-Bound Robust Bidding of Renewable-Based Virtual Power Plants
papers.summary: RVPPs that aggregate dispatchable and non-dispatchable renewable energy sources, storage, and flexible demand that bid in the day-ahead and secondary reserve markets must cope with uncertainties in market prices, renewable generation, and demand. MBRO is well suited to this setting because it hedges adverse realizations through several deviation layers while keeping the final bidding problem as a tractable, scenario-free MILP. Its performance, however, depends on how the deviation bounds and uncertainty budgets are calibrated. Existing MBRO implementations commonly rely on fixed percentile-based bounds and externally specified budget vectors, usually examined through sensitivity analysis. This paper proposes PL-MBRO, that constructs parameter-specific deviation bounds from historical data conditional on selected risk-attitude quantiles and automatically derives the corresponding uncertainty budgets from empirical cluster probabilities. For each uncertain parameter, k-medians clustering partitions the historical daily profiles into representative probability layers; the cluster median defines the balanced representative, while favorable and adverse within-cluster percentiles define the optimistic and pessimistic representatives. The empirical cluster probabilities are mapped to integer full-horizon uncertainty budgets over the 96 quarter-hourly periods, while the robust inner problem determines the periods in which the corresponding deviation layers are most adverse to the schedule. Compared with a percentilebased MBRO benchmark, in-sample and out-of-sample tests on an RVPP bidding in both markets show that PL-MBRO consistently achieves better realized economic outcomes across the optimistic, balanced, and pessimistic strategies, with improvements of up to 92.7% in-sample and 57.3% out-of-sample, measured relative to the absolute value of the corresponding benchmark realized profit.

papers.title: Delta-Seeker: Closed-Loop Generative Search for Novel Circuit Design Discovery
papers.summary: Generative models are increasingly used for circuit synthesis and optimization by proposing topologies, sizing devices, and exploring large design spaces. We investigate whether they can instead support design discovery, where generated structures must depart from known designs while producing reproducible electrical behavior. We propose Delta-Seeker, a closed-loop circuit search framework that combines discrete diffusion for topology generation and mutation with structural checking, SPICE-in-the-loop sizing, Pareto selection, and feedback from prior search outcomes. The search controller uses progress and recurring structural failures to allocate evaluation effort and steer subsequent topology generation, while independent re-sizing and operating-corner analysis are performed only after search. In generator-only experiments, cross-generation feedback increases structurally valid children from 143 to 945 and reduces the faulty-candidate fraction from 0.925 to 0.761. In op-amp topology discovery at matched sizing cost, Delta-Seeker yields 54 designs that remain feasible in at least three of four independent re-sizings and 18 that additionally pass device-level checks and supply-temperature corner analysis, compared with 38 and 10 under fixed control. Removing cross-generation memory reduces independently robust discoveries from 54 to 43 and seven-corner robust discoveries from 40 to 27. In DC-DC converter search, nearest-parent analysis identifies a corpus-absent topology whose generated switching current path changes its nearest training-corpus parent from infeasible at all four operating corners to feasible at all four, while increasing median efficiency from 31.2% to 98.96%. These results show that closed-loop generative search can support circuit discovery beyond structural novelty by identifying new topologies with independently verified changes in circuit operation.

papers.title: Koopman--Lyapunov and Koopman--Riccati Controller Synthesis
papers.summary: While the Koopman operator-based lifted representations of nonlinear autonomous and controlled systems have been well covered in the literature, the direct controller synthesis problem largely remains open. As the controlled system is generally a bilinear (instead of fully linear) Koopman model, controller synthesis appears to lose the linear--quadratic structures of the classical Lyapunov and Riccati methods for finite-dimensional linear systems. However, in infinite dimensions, bilinearity in the feature map should be merely artifactual and hence reducible to linearity in principle. In this work, by considering the operator semigroups in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space with a linear--Sobolev kernel and utilizing the Yosida approximation of their generators, the synthesis problems of a stabilizing controller and an input-unconstrained optimal controller can be formulated as an operator Lyapunov inequality and an operator Riccati equation, respectively. These formulations recover the desirable linear--quadratic structures, and hence, with sample data, they are solvable efficiently in analogous ways to usual linear systems by semidefinite programming solvers and Kleinman iterations, respectively. In addition to proving control performance bounds dependent on the sampling denseness and Yosida regularization, through numerical comparison to linearized LQR, bilinear EDMD-based synthesis, nonlinear MPC, and Koopman MPC methods on numerical models and process control examples, this work demonstrates the proposed Koopman--Riccati synthesis as a computationally efficient approach to obtain a near-optimal state-feedback control law.

papers.title: Machine learning-guided real-time AC optimal transmission switching
papers.summary: The operation of power grids has substantial economic consequences, affecting generation costs and, ultimately, electricity prices. papers.title: Low-rank corrections to a shared reference Jacobian for GPU-parallel AC $N\!-\!1$ contingency analysis
papers.summary: Contingency analysis repeatedly solves the power-flow equations under many single-element outages, an increasingly demanding workload as operating margins tighten and renewable variability grows. This paper presents a GPU-parallel Newton--Raphson solver for $N\!-\!1$ contingency analysis that separates the change in operating state from the change in topology. A single reference Jacobian is inverted once and reused across all contingencies. Each topology change is expressed as a low-rank Woodbury correction, while the residual state-dependent perturbation is handled by an inner iterative solve, a truncated Neumann series or the biconjugate gradient stabilized method. We analyze the spectral radius and condition number of the resulting iteration matrices and show that the reference Jacobian is an effective preconditioner. On transmission-scale benchmarks, the method attains per-topology solve times competitive with an optimized 80-core central processing unit baseline, with the low-rank correction accounting for approximately 1--2\% of the workload. This makes GPU-parallel $N\!-\!1$ contingency analysis feasible at transmission scale without per-topology refactorization.

papers.title: Shadow Pricing of Static Voltage Stability Services within Unit Commitment for Inverter-Dominated Power Systems
papers.summary: Modern power systems are increasingly dominated by Inverter-Based Resources (IBR), most of which work in Grid-following (GFL) mode. Using a modified IEEE 30-bus system, we demonstrate that both the dispatchable and restricted pricing methods can yield revenue-adequate service prices, though the former may deliver less efficient price signals and the latter may require well-defined uplift payments. papers.title: Protection challenges and solutions on power systems towards 100% inverter-based resources and energy storage systems
papers.summary: The decarbonization of the energy sector, driven by the Paris Agreement and the European Green Deal, is increasing the share of renewable energy sources (RES) in power systems. Unlike traditional systems, RES-based systems rely on power electronic converters, which creates unprecedented challenges for reliability and resilience. The future power system is expected to combine a low-level AC layer with an upper-level High Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) backbone, which requires new understanding of fault protection, stability, and interaction between AC and DC components, as well as new models and simulation tools. This is especially critical in systems moving towards 100 percent converter-based generation. Protection systems detect, locate, and isolate faults to protect assets while the rest of the system keeps operating. Traditionally, they rely on the large fault currents supplied by synchronous machines. In modern systems, converter controls limit the fault current contribution to about 120 percent of rated current, so relays that distinguish faults from normal overcurrents based on current level may operate incorrectly. In addition, inverter-based resources (IBR) may not inject enough negative and zero sequence current for directional relays to work properly, and converters hold the voltage at a fixed value only within their reach, beyond which it drops quickly. As a result, existing protection schemes may not provide the expected accuracy and reliability. This report reviews the protection challenges identified in recent academic literature for power systems with high shares of converter-based resources. It covers the specific characteristics of RES, the challenges for protection with intelligent electronic devices (IED), the challenges of converter control during faults, and the main solutions proposed in research over the last decade.

papers.title: Orion: Enabling Self-adaptive Memory Management for On-device Online Continual Learning
papers.summary: Online continual learning (OCL) enables real-time adaptation to new data, making it crucial for dynamic robotic applications. To further demonstrate its practical utility, Orion is integrated into a realistic autonomous navigational robot powered by OCL. The results show that Orion achieves significant training speedups while maintaining balanced performance and effectively adapting to various scenarios, all with minimal runtime, memory, and energy overhead, making Orion a practical solution for on-device continual learning.

papers.title: Finding optimal measurement sequences for broken or constrained measuring devices

papers.title: Global Parameter Identification and Uncertainty Quantification of reduced-order ADM1 using Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Bayesian Inference

These are refined by the Gauss-Newton algorithm as the best local search, which delivers $R^2$ values of 0.95 for acetic acid and 0.77 for biogas production. BI yields substantially narrower uncertainty bands than MLE and avoids the need for a global search by incorporating prior knowledge about parameter distributions. The search space is captured efficiently by log10 scaling of parameters. Algorithmic details on its implications are provided. papers.summary: We study the problem of selecting the fewest admissible input--state links that make a structured linear system structurally controllable. papers.title: QFabric: Guarded Cross-Domain Task Recovery and Its Limits on a Linux-RTOS Board

papers.title: Why the Swing Parameters Are Sloppy

papers.title: On the Degree of Safety: Beyond Safe or Unsafe with Control Barrier Functions
papers.summary: A valid control barrier function (CBF) certifies if its represented safe set can be rendered forward invariant, and the sign of its value indicates whether a state is safe or not, but it does not quantify a degree of safety beyond the binary indication. papers.summary: Game-theoretic models are increasingly used to describe multi-agent interactions in control and robotics applications. We show that our algorithm can commit 56 generators for 200 days 10,000 times faster than Hexaly, the leading commercial solver for scheduling problems, without sacrificing solution quality. We attain this runtime improvement by introducing a greedy-heuristic tailored for hydro units. We provide a direction for a possible proof that the error our solver makes decreases with the problem size. This is supported by our experimental results. We prove that our solver's runtime scales log-linearly in the number of generators and time periods.

papers.title: Incremental Stability of Gradient Flows under Generalized Polyak-Łojasiewicz Inequalities and Its Implications for General Systems
papers.summary: Gradient flows of twice continuously differentiable strongly convex and convex objectives are, respectively, incrementally exponentially stable and non-expansive in the Euclidean metric. In this work, we investigate to what extent these properties extend to nonconvex objectives satisfying generalized Polyak-Łojasiewicz inequalities. For objectives with a unique minimizer, we establish conditions under which the gradient flow is contracting in a state-dependent Riemannian metric and incrementally exponentially stable. For objectives with nonunique minimizers, we generalize the non-expansivity of convex objectives to incremental stability for more general nonconvex objectives. We focus on incremental stability due to its implication to convergence to equilibrium points; when paired with a Lyapunov function it implies pointwise convergence to a minimizer and continuity of the endpoint map. Along the way, we derive new structural results for incrementally stable nonlinear systems and extend the analysis to Heavy-Ball and Dynamical Inertial Newton flows.

papers.title: Dynamic Persuasion: Managing Reputation under Censored Feedback
papers.summary: We study a long-run sender who repeatedly communicates about a state to a sequence of myopic receivers and whose credibility is a public score updated from past interactions. Receivers face a lemon loss and an opportunity loss, and their behavior depends on these only through a single index, the tolerance. Because the score records only detected misrepresentations, it rests above the sender's true honesty rate; we characterize this credibility premium in closed form. In a fluid limit in which the score adjusts slowly, no policy earns more than operating at a single credibility level, and the sender's gain from managing credibility equals the value of the premium: against receivers who correct for imperfect detection, that gain vanishes. At a fixed adjustment speed, every policy is bounded by the fluid value plus a term linear in the speed. We then study three policy classes, linear, (s,S), and threshold, obtain the optimal parameters of the linear and threshold classes in closed form, show how receiver losses shape them, and show that, under an approximation, the optimal (s,S) band collapses to a threshold. Simulations of the dynamics agree with the closed forms and indicate where the single-level conclusion stops: bands pay when switching modes is costly, and cycles pay when demand is seasonal.

papers.title: Quantifying Linepack Storage Potential of Hydrogen Networks

papers.title: Analog Realization and Measurement of a Forced Aliev-Panfilov Excitable Oscillator
papers.summary: A single resistor moves a discrete analog realization of the forced Aliev-Panfilov excitable oscillator from a chaotic operating point of the model to a regular one. The input resistor of the excitation integrator sets that parameter, so no state, delay element, or controller is added. Sampled waveforms were recorded at two resistor values, with two independent runs each. The measured excitation excursion agrees with numerical integration to within three percent at the baseline setting and five percent at the rate-controlled setting. Between the two settings the excitation excursion contracts by a factor of thirteen. At the rate-controlled setting the recovery excursion exceeds prediction by a factor of eight. This excess traces to a displaced operating point on the state-dependent recovery rate. Thermal drift in the multiplier chain and leakage at the high-impedance recovery-rate divider could each produce it, and the present data do not separate them. A tested bipolar input stage strongly loads that divider, a constraint absent from the ideal equations. The divider, not the sub-hertz signal bandwidth, sets the amplifier input-stage requirement.

papers.title: A Behavioral approach to Constrained Linear Quadratic Control: Feasibility and Optimality
papers.summary: This paper develops a constrained linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control framework within the behavioral approach. Unlike classical formulations that rely on state-input representations, our method treats both the system dynamics and the constraints as trajectory-level objects. papers.title: Biased Stochastic Gradient Descent under Local Geometry, with Application to Data-Driven LQR
papers.summary: We study stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with biased stochastic gradient oracles for objectives that are only locally smooth and locally gradient dominated, with constants that may grow with the objective value and are required only on a sublevel set. We illustrate the framework on the linear quadratic regulator (LQR), whose cost satisfies these properties only on sublevel sets and whose policy gradient depends on the unknown system matrices. We consider an indirect estimator, which identifies the system matrices online, and a direct zeroth-order estimator. We characterize the bias and the second moment of both estimators and show how to choose their parameters so that the convergence conditions hold. On an event of prescribed probability, both data-driven policy gradient methods converge to the optimal policy almost surely and in expectation, with guarantees for all iterations rather than at a single prescribed iteration. We compare the two estimators, and numerical experiments on the LQR illustrate the results.

papers.title: A heuristic for optimal coordination of autonomous vehicles: real-time algorithms

papers.title: A heuristic for optimal coordination of autonomous vehicles: dynamic problems

papers.title: Safe Platooning under Input Constraints with Link-Wise Velocity String Stability

papers.title: Which wind and solar modelling choices matter? Effects on capacity factors, energy droughts and European power system configuration
papers.summary: Europe's future power system will rely heavily on wind and solar power and must remain resilient during prolonged periods of low wind and solar generation, known as variable renewable energy (VRE) droughts. To capture such rare events, adequacy assessments increasingly draw on decades of weather data, but the conversion of weather into power is largely treated as fixed. It remains unclear which modelling choices in this conversion matter for representing these droughts, and whether they matter as much as the weather itself. Here we systematically compare these choices side by side (bias correction, wind speed extrapolation, capacity layouts, turbine and photovoltaic configurations, and wake losses) and trace their effects through VRE droughts to the design of a net-zero European power system, using 85 years of reanalysis data. We find that modelling choices barely change how often VRE droughts occur or when the system is stressed. They do, however, determine how much capacity is needed to withstand that stress. By altering the electricity delivered during droughts, they shift required capacity by up to 480 GW, which is comparable to the spread across the most critical weather years. Modelling exercises should therefore use multiple weather years; bias-correct and regionally validate weather inputs; explicitly represent resource heterogeneity, forward-looking technologies, and wake losses; and judge these choices by their effect on the low-generation tail, not only on the mean.

papers.title: Neuromorphic design of a rhythmic network
papers.summary: Central Pattern Generators (CPGs) have long inspired the design of rhythms that combine endogenous generation and exogenous interaction. In neurodynamics and engineering studies, CPGs have been primarily analysed and designed as networks of coupled oscillators. In contrast, the present article regards CPGs as networks that propagate events through excitable rather than oscillatory nodes. The proposed event-based perspective reduces the design of network-level rhythmic properties to the tuning of local nodal input-output characteristics. This reduction enables a distributed and robust design methodology: nodes can be tuned independently, they can be heterogeneous, and the global rhythm results from local event propagation rather than from a specific global tuning of the network parameters. The present article builds on previously introduced concepts that parallel existing characterizations of oscillators: the event describing function (eDF), which characterises the propagation delay of a node, and the event phase response curve (ePRC), which characterises the phase sensitivity of a node. Event-based CPGs made of excitable rather than oscillatory nodes emerge as a principled design framework for robust rhythm generation.

papers.title: Computing with Coupled Oscillator Networks: Optimization, Memory, and Modern AI Primitives
papers.summary: We explore how synchronization in coupled oscillator networks may be employed to perform a variety of computing tasks. These systems are becoming more attractive as an alternative to conventional digital computers due to the increasing energy demands of the latter, particularly for large-scale problems in machine learning and artificial intelligence. The ubiquity of coupled oscillator networks means that oscillator-based computing can be thought of as a universal computing paradigm encompassing systems with a diversity of physical realizations, e.g. as analog circuits, neurological systems, spintronic systems. The bridge between the dynamics of coupled oscillator networks and computational primitives they implement is the Ising model, which originates in statistical physics, and when applied to oscillator networks, explains the emergence of globally complex and disordered synchronization patterns from local interactions in the network. We discuss the application of coupled oscillator networks to three fundamental computing operations. First, oscillator networks as specialized hardware solvers of NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, with the solution encoded in the synchrony patterns. Second, oscillator networks as associative memory systems, enabling storage and retrieval of data represented through phases of oscillations. Finally, oscillator networks as a dynamical implementation of attention, with synchronization providing the mechanism for the alignment of keys to queries. The ability of oscillator networks to implement these computational primitives paves the way for novel realizations of intelligent systems through a variety of physical substrates.

papers.title: Reachability-Augmented Dual Dynamic Programming for Optimal Path Parameterization
papers.summary: Optimal path parameterization (OPP) is a fundamental problem for planning trajectories along a prescribed geometric path under kinodynamic constraints and task-dependent objectives. papers.title: Smoothing the Ramp, Not the Peak: Scheduling-Induced Power Dynamics of LLM Inference and Their Grid-Scale Consequences

papers.title: DriftingPlanner: Drifting Generative Models for One-Step Trajectory Planning in End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.summary: End-to-end planners decode the ego trajectory either by coordinate regression, which is fast but blends plausible maneuvers into one trajectory that may follow none of them, or by diffusion and flow matching, which model the trajectory distribution but need several inference steps. Drifting models move this iteration into training: a one-step generator learns to follow an attraction--repulsion field between generated and ground-truth samples. Drifting was developed for class-conditional image generation, where every class supplies many positive samples. In planning, every scene is its own condition. Pooling scenes would attract the generated trajectories of one scene to the ground truth of unrelated scenes, whereas computing the field per scene leaves a single positive, the expert trajectory. Mutual repulsion then holds the generated trajectories on a shell around it, so any single generated trajectory deviates from the ground truth. We present DriftingPlanner, a trajectory planner trained with the drifting loss alone, without any coordinate regression term. It computes the field per scene and removes the shell at inference: it decodes every noise vector together with its negation in one batched pass, and averaging each antithetic pair cancels the linear part of the displacement from the shell center. On NAVSIM navtest, DriftingPlanner reaches a state-of-the-art 93.75 PDMS, and with single-step inference its drifting decoder comes within 0.13 PDMS of the best diffusion or flow matching setting, which needs ten inference steps.

papers.title: Lexicographic Descent: A Gradient-Based Approach to Optimize Totally Ordered Rulebooks via Parametric Scalarization
papers.summary: Safety-critical systems, such as autonomous vehicles, must satisfy conflicting constraints and objectives, collectively called rules, typically ordered lexicographically. Preemptive lexicographic optimization solves a sequence of problems, one per priority level. However, higher levels are optimized without considering lower ones, making the approach susceptible to suboptimal solutions. On the other hand, scalarization optimizes all levels jointly and so avoids this myopia, but a finite weighted sum permits trade-offs across priority levels, and exact scalar representations lack the regularity standard solvers require. We propose Lexicographic Descent, which combines the benefits of both: a single weighted sum whose relative weights decay at priority-dependent rates, recovering the lexicographic order in the limit. We show that Lexicographic Descent converges to constrained stationary points of the highest-priority rule, matching preemptive guarantees. Since the lower-priority weights vanish, we derive a necessary condition for the lower-priority rules to keep guiding the iterates, with the aim of avoiding suboptimal stationary points of the higher-priority rules. We show that Lexicographic Descent can exploit problem structure to reach the lexicographic optima, and outperforms the preemptive approach on an autonomous driving case study.

papers.title: Safety4DM: A Vision-Language Framework for Risk-Aware Dynamic Maps in Vehicle-Road-Cloud Collaborative Driving
papers.summary: Dynamic map (DM) is a core information infrastructure for vehicle-road-cloud (VRC) cooperative autonomous driving. It fuses perception data from multiple sources to overcome the inherent line-of-sight and field-of-view limits of single-vehicle perception. However, DM still falls short on driving safety in two ways. First, DM data specifications already define road conditions semantically, but no pipeline yet turns real-world road observations into fine-grained risk entities in the DM. Second, existing DM systems lack a natural language interface for driving risks. To close these gaps, we propose Safety4DM, a safety-oriented language system for VRC dynamic maps. We first build RoadRisk, a real-world road image dataset that covers four types of road conditions and four risk levels. On this dataset, we fine-tune a vision-language model (VLM) for road safety risk perception. The model outputs structured risk representations that the DM can ingest directly. We then introduce a Safety-aware Step-wise Prompting (SafeStep) mechanism as the natural language query interface of the DM. SafeStep answers queries accurately and also generates actionable driving advice. To build and evaluate this interface, we develop SafeVRC-Sim, a VRC cooperative simulation framework, and SafeDM-QA, a safety question-answering benchmark. Experiments show that even the compact Qwen3-VL-4B reaches 89.83% accuracy on risk perception after fine-tuning. SafeStep also plugs easily into multiple LLM families. With medium and large models (20B and above) from five families, it achieves over 93% natural language query accuracy in every case, which shows strong generalization.

papers.title: Leveraging 2D Foundation Priors for Generalized Category Discovery under Test-Time Adaptation in 3D LiDAR Segmentation
papers.summary: In autonomous driving, 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation is expected to adapt to evolving environments and recognize previously unseen categories, making generalized category discovery under test-time adaptation (GCD-TTA) an important problem. However, existing works treat GCD and TTA separately, while the limited semantic information in 3D point clouds makes GCD-TTA under domain shift more prone to feature collapse when combining GCD with TTA. To address this issue, we propose a two-stage framework for GCD-TTA in 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation. Specifically, in the first stage, we adaptively aggregate local 3D features according to geometric density variations and obtain reliable pseudo labels under a global class-wise prototype consistency constraint. In the second stage, we cast category discovery as an optimal transport assignment process for globally consistent grouping of novel categories. Meanwhile, semantic features from 2D vision foundation models are fused with 3D point cloud features to enrich 3D semantic information and promote a more separable feature space. Extensive experiments on Synth4D to SemanticKITTI, SynLiDAR to SemanticKITTI, and Synth4D to nuScenes demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework. Under a unified evaluation protocol, our method achieves the best overall mIoU on 9 out of 10 benchmark splits and improves the overall mIoU by up to 12.21 points over the strongest re-implemented baseline.

papers.title: Kernel-Gradient Drifting Models
papers.summary: We propose kernel-gradient drifting, a one-step generative modeling framework that replaces the fixed Euclidean displacement direction in drifting models with directions induced by the kernel itself. Standard drifting is attractive because it enables fast, high-quality generation without distilling a large pretrained diffusion model, but its theory is currently understood mainly for Gaussian kernels, where the drift coincides with smoothed score matching and is identifiable. Our gradient-based reformulation exposes this score-based structure for general kernels: the resulting drift is the score difference between kernel-smoothed data and model distributions, yielding identifiability for characteristic kernels and a smoothed-KL descent interpretation of the smoothed drifting dynamics. Since kernel gradients are intrinsic tangent vectors, the same construction extends naturally to Riemannian manifolds and to discrete data via the Fisher-Rao geometry of the probability simplex. Across spherical geospatial data, promoter DNA and molecule generation, kernel-gradient drifting enables state-of-the-art one-step generation beyond the Euclidean setting without distillation. Code is available \href{https://github.com/jcarrascopollo/kgd_thesis}{here}.

papers.title: A/B Agent: A Self-Evolving Agent for Strategy Iteration in Industrial A/B Testing
papers.summary: Industrial recommendation strategy iteration heavily relies on large-scale A/B experimentation. Traditional tuning requires experts to repeatedly design strategies, configure experiments, analyze results, and adjust parameters, making the process labor-intensive and time-consuming. Meanwhile, valuable knowledge from historical experiments is often fragmented, making systematic reuse difficult through manual expert effort alone. Existing RAG agents partially alleviate this burden by retrieving prior strategies, but typically organize experience in a flat manner, overlooking the hierarchical relationships among business scenarios, recommendation stages, optimization objectives, and experimental contexts. This often results in mismatched retrieval and limited cross-scenario transfer, while preventing agents from continuously refining strategies and parameters through sequential A/B feedback. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{\ourname}, a closed-loop A/B agent for industrial recommendation strategy optimization. The framework comprises three tightly coupled core components: \textit{Historical Strategy Knowledge Organization}, \textit{Autonomous Target-Aware Strategy Generation}, and \textit{Experiment-Guided Strategy Self-Evolution}. It organizes historical strategies into a hierarchical experience tree, retrieves transferable evidence through multi-path Tree-RAG to generate executable strategies, and continuously analyzes online A/B feedback to guide autonomous tuning and update the experience tree for self-evolution. Extensive offline and online evaluations demonstrate its effectiveness, including a \textbf{4.829%} improvement in GMV in a real-world short-video e-commerce recommendation system while maintaining positive gains across all guardrail metrics.

papers.title: Fair Recommender Systems for Intersecting Groups
papers.summary: Recommendation systems that optimize for the average user can fail to capture the preferences of diverse demographic groups. We consider a dynamic recommendation system, where arriving users can belong to different demographic groups. Importantly, these groups can intersect, and a user may belong to several groups. We first show that over time, any group-blind policy (which excludes all current-user group information) recommending $K \geq 1$ items incurs linear total regret under mild conditions. In turn, we introduce three group-aware algorithms based on the classical Upper Confidence Bound algorithm (UCB): i) Intersection-Fitting, which runs UCB on each intersection, but has a sublinear group- and intersection-level regret guarantee with an exponential dependence in the number of groups; and ii) two group-level heuristics, Inner-Outer UCB and Group-Item UCB which allocate different arms to different groups, and use a sleeping expert meta-learner to choose which active group's recommendation an intersection should inherit at any given time step. We provide experimental results on two datasets, Goodreads and BoardGameGeek, and highlight that our heuristics can be preferable to the intersection-fitting algorithm when intersection-level preferences are closely related to group-level preferences, but that intersection-fitting performs better when different intersections within a same group prefer different items.

papers.title: TACFormer: Transformer-Based Generative Model for Target-Conditioned De Novo PROTAC Design
papers.summary: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) represents a fundamental shift in drug discovery, moving beyond traditional target inhibition toward the event-driven removal of disease-causing proteins. A prominent strategy for TPD is the use of proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), heterobifunctional molecules that selectively route a protein of interest (POI) to the ubiquitin-proteasome system for degradation. While PROTAC design still relies heavily on trial-and-error synthesis and experimental testing, deep generative models offer a promising means to explore PROTAC chemical space in silico and generate novel molecules. However, many existing generative methods formulate PROTAC design primarily as a linker-generation problem, with POI-binding (warhead) and E3-ligase-binding components fixed in advance. This restricts exploration of the full PROTAC chemical space and often leaves the POI implicit through the predefined warhead, rather than using protein-level information as an explicit conditioning signal during generation. To address these limitations, we propose TACFormer: a transformer-based generative model for target-aware de novo PROTAC design. The model conditions a GPT-style molecular decoder on pretrained ESM-2 representations of POI sequences, allowing POI-level information to steer full-molecule generation. Our results show that TACFormer generates highly novel and chemically diverse PROTACs while showing consistent POI-dependent shifts in generated chemical space. In particular, molecules generated under specific target conditions preferentially populate chemical neighborhoods associated with POIs in the held-out dataset, while extrapolating to novel chemotypes. By natively integrating biological context into the generative process, TACFormer moves PROTAC design toward a more biology-informed exploration of degrader chemical space.

papers.title: LiDAR-SHIELD: A Fully Dockerized Adversarial Robustness Assessment Framework for LiDAR-Based 3D Perception Models
papers.summary: LiDAR-based 3D perception underpins autonomous driving and robotics, yet deploying these models safely requires stress-testing them against adversarial inputs before real-world use. Although state-of-the-art adversarial attacks exist, their implementations are often fragmented across individual repositories, each tied to a specific architecture or task and requiring manual environment reconstruction and model-specific integration code. We present LIDARSHIELD, a unified and fully Dockerized framework that reverses this workflow: rather than installing the target model inside the toolkit, LIDARSHIELD exposes any model through three lightweight HTTP endpoints, namely /info, /forward, and /gradient As a result, connecting a new model or dataset requires only a single loader function or adapter. The framework supports both 3D semantic segmentation and 3D object detection through the same engine-service protocol, integrating a task-aware suite of state-of-the-art attacks, including PGD and Square Attack for segmentation, and point perturbation, point removal, point injection, and LiDAttack for detection. This enables systematic exposure of corner cases and vulnerabilities across heterogeneous LiDAR backbones. The LiDAR-Shield codebase is publicly available at https://github.com/alexandrosgk/LiDAR-shield.

papers.title: On the Performance of AoA-Based Physical-Layer Authentication Under Multi-Source Impersonation Attacks
papers.summary: This paper investigates cooperative impersonation attacks against angle-of-arrival (AoA)-based authentication for a wireless communication receiver equipped with a digital uniform linear array. Specifically, we characterize the vulnerability and robustness of this authentication system in relation to adversarial angular diversity and the relative numbers of adversarial sources and receive antennas. To this end, we first derive the optimal precoding vector for multiple spatially distributed adversarial sources by minimizing the mean squared error between legitimate and adversarial received signals. By means of the rank property of Vandermonde matrices, we then establish necessary and sufficient conditions under which the adversarial sources can reproduce the legitimate transmitter's spatial signature. With fewer adversarial sources than receive antennas, perfect reproduction is not possible without at least one adversarial source satisfying a specific AoA condition. In the other case, increasing the number of receive antennas can reduce impersonation success probabilities when none of the adversarial sources has an AoA satisfying this condition. Numerical results validate the theoretical analysis and evaluate the security performance of AoA-based authentication.

papers.title: Structured Representation Probing for Risk Anticipation in End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.summary: End-to-end driving policies form structured internal representations of traffic, ego behavior, and road constraints. These representations offer a monitoring interface for anticipating failures, complementing risk signals from trajectories, controls, and manually designed features. We introduce the Structured Representation Probe (SRP), a lightweight monitor that reads actor, ego, and map representations from a frozen policy. SRP learns a separate linear risk direction for each source and aggregates element scores through cardinality-normalized log-mean-exp pooling, retaining sensitivity to salient evidence while reducing dependence on token count. Event-window supervision links the readout to upcoming hard failures, and auxiliary event type heads jointly train the source directions across failure modes. Online alerting uses a single generic score without modifying the driving policy. Bench2Drive experiments on DriveTransformer, UniAD, and VAD show higher frame-level PR-AUC and ROC-AUC than the evaluated runtime baselines. On DriveTransformer at a horizon of 2 seconds, ROC-AUC reaches 0.833 versus 0.715 for temporal consistency, with 2.67% readout runtime overhead. The trained probes also retain the ability to distinguish impending failures on new routes.
